status: Ready: two additional motion and creative-coding profiles; existing profiles are unchanged
editorialNote: Original educational analysis of public, bylined sources. Documented decisions are distinguished from editorial alternatives and tradeoffs. Exercises are original practice suggestions, not assignments endorsed by the practitioners. Historical browser-support statements are not current compatibility advice. Sources remain their authors' property; inclusion implies no endorsement.

people.name: Matt Perry
people.focus: Animation architecture, responsive interaction, and explicit performance tradeoffs
people.keyIdea: Choose animation machinery for the interaction it must preserve, then explain the rendering costs and failure cases rather than treating smoothness as magic.

artifacts.title: Crashing cars and improving hover detection
artifacts.author: Matt Perry
artifacts.sourceType: Bylined implementation essay with comparative demos
artifacts.summary: Explains skipped hover targets through discrete pointer sampling, then applies line-segment collision testing and grouped geometry reads to a showcase grid.

artifacts.title: Building the ultimate ticker
artifacts.author: Matt Perry
artifacts.sourceType: Bylined component design rationale and commercial announcement
artifacts.summary: Describes Motion+ Ticker's item recycling, velocity-based animation, visibility controls, reduced-motion behavior, and an explicitly provisional keyboard-navigation approach.

artifacts.title: The Web Animation Performance Tier List
artifacts.author: Matt Perry
artifacts.summary: Organizes animation approaches by rendering work and execution thread, while discussing layer memory, layout reads, and exceptions to simple performance rankings.

artifacts.title: Do you still need Framer Motion?
artifacts.author: Matt Perry
artifacts.sourceType: Bylined historical comparison of native CSS and a JavaScript animation library
artifacts.summary: Compares native animation capabilities with library behavior, including the difference between a sampled spring-like curve and velocity-aware, interruptible spring motion.

decisions.decision: Test the segment between previous and current pointer positions against target rectangles.
decisions.alternative: React only when a sampled pointer position lands inside a target.
decisions.tradeoff: Fast swipes reach otherwise skipped targets, but geometry measurement and intersection checks add work.

decisions.decision: Recycle ticker items across the visible boundary and create only the clones required by the measured viewport.
decisions.alternative: Duplicate a fixed item set or provision for the widest possible viewport.
decisions.tradeoff: Less duplicated content reduces overhead, at the cost of measurement and item-positioning logic.
decisions.status: Documented component design; complexity tradeoff is editorial analysis

decisions.decision: Expose ticker velocity in pixels per second and drive its offset on the main thread.
decisions.alternative: Use a fixed-duration CSS loop whose speed changes with content length.
decisions.tradeoff: Speed stays intelligible and supports gesture composition, but scheduling becomes vulnerable to main-thread contention.
decisions.status: Documented component choice; contention consequence is editorial analysis

decisions.decision: Apply layer-promotion hints deliberately rather than adding will-change to every animated element.
decisions.alternative: Treat blanket layer promotion as a universal performance fix.
decisions.tradeoff: Promotion can avoid paint for suitable updates, but excessive or oversized layers consume GPU memory.
decisions.status: Author's stated recommendation and Motion implementation rationale

decisions.decision: Preserve incoming velocity when a spring animation follows a gesture or interrupted animation.
decisions.alternative: Replay a predefined spring-shaped easing curve from a new starting point.
decisions.tradeoff: Velocity-aware behavior supports continuity; a fixed curve can be a simpler, lightweight choice for self-contained motion.
decisions.status: Documented library behavior and author's comparison, not a universal selection rule

writingTechniques.technique: Let readers experience the defect before naming the algorithm.
writingTechniques.evidence: Two hover grids establish a perceptual difference before the essay connects pointer sampling to tunnelling in game physics.

writingTechniques.technique: Use the same problem categories to structure the critique and proposed solution.
writingTechniques.evidence: The ticker article revisits responsiveness, accessibility, and animation in the same order, making the component's claimed remedies easy to audit.

writingTechniques.technique: Teach the mechanism before offering a memorable classification.
writingTechniques.evidence: The performance article introduces rendering stages and threads before assigning tiers, then adds caveats that prevent the ranking from replacing judgment.

exercise.task: Prototype one reversible panel transition using a fixed easing curve and a velocity-aware spring. Keep distance and visual styling equal. Reverse each at early, middle, and late points; record the response with and without a controlled main-thread workload. Add a reduced-motion version and write when you would choose each implementation.
exercise.deliverable: Two original prototypes, a six-case interruption matrix, browser and device details, and a 250-word decision note separating measured results from perceived continuity.
evaluation: Does reversal preserve a convincing trajectory without delaying the requested state change?
Are claims backed by repeatable traces or recordings rather than a tier label alone?
Can the interface remain understandable with motion disabled?

limitations: Perry authors the articles and created Motion; this does not establish sole authorship of every component or dependency.
The ticker article is also marketing. Its keyboard approach is explicitly described as work in progress, not a proven accessibility standard.
The hover demonstration approximates movement as straight segments between samples and checks rectangles; it does not reconstruct the true continuous path.
Performance depends on browser, device, layer size, and workload. No demos, paid components, or benchmark claims were independently executed here.
The CSS comparison dates from 2024 and contains historical support and implementation statements. Recheck current documentation before implementation.
people.coverage: Four bylined primary artifacts reviewed, with five concrete decisions, three communication techniques, and an original interruption-testing exercise.

people.name: jhey
people.focus: Creative coding, parametric CSS, and teaching through inspectable experiments
people.keyIdea: Turn a striking effect into a small set of understandable inputs, expose how those inputs work, and keep the result adaptable to devices and user preferences.

artifacts.title: Parallax Powered by CSS Custom Properties
artifacts.author: Jhey Tompkins
artifacts.sourceType: Author-published syndication of a first-person implementation tutorial
artifacts.summary: Separates pointer input from per-object visual coefficients in a parallax scene, with configurable motion reduction and non-hover behavior.

artifacts.title: Building Chrometober!
artifacts.author: Jhey Tompkins
artifacts.sourceType: Bylined team-project retrospective; date is the displayed last-updated date
artifacts.summary: Documents a scrolling-book project, its responsive concept change, component architecture, accessibility review, and experimental API feedback. Team responsibilities are explicitly credited.

artifacts.title: Speedy CSS Tip! Animated Loader
artifacts.author: Jhey Tompkins
artifacts.sourceType: Bylined compact CSS tutorial; date is the displayed last-updated date
artifacts.summary: Builds a radial loader from count and index custom properties, calculated geometry and opacity, and a matching stepped rotation.

artifacts.title: The Path To Awesome CSS Easing With The linear() Function
artifacts.author: Jhey Tompkins
artifacts.sourceType: Bylined technical tutorial and tool-building account
artifacts.summary: Explains custom easing through visual examples and recounts simplifying a GSAP-to-CSS conversion tool with Jake Archibald's help.

decisions.decision: Pass two normalized pointer values into scoped CSS properties; configure each object's response separately.
decisions.alternative: Calculate every object's visual transform in the pointer handler.
decisions.tradeoff: Input logic stays reusable, while CSS coefficient relationships require careful naming and tuning.
decisions.status: Documented implementation; alternative and maintenance tradeoff are editorial analysis

decisions.decision: Replace the initial sideways scene-navigation concept with a scrolling 3D book.
decisions.alternative: Continue developing rotating and scaling scenes along a horizontal route.
decisions.tradeoff: The book better matched the team's responsive ambitions, while retaining substantial page-turning and accessibility complexity.
decisions.status: Jhey's documented concept decision; remaining complexity is editorial analysis

decisions.decision: Derive radial loader geometry, opacity, and stepped rotation from shared count and index values.
decisions.alternative: Hand-author separate placement and timing values for every spoke.
decisions.tradeoff: One parameter system supports variation, but generated markup and the declared count must stay synchronized.
decisions.status: Documented tutorial implementation; alternative and synchronization caution are editorial analysis

decisions.decision: Convert GSAP easing functions directly instead of extracting and rescaling SVG paths from its visualizer.
decisions.alternative: Continue using an intermediate geometric representation of the easing curve.
decisions.tradeoff: Direct function input removes conversion work; generated point simplification still trades output size against approximation fidelity.
decisions.status: Documented simplification prompted by Jake Archibald; fidelity tradeoff is editorial analysis

decisions.decision: Multiply decorative parallax transforms by a shared motion coefficient and set it to zero when hovering is unavailable.
decisions.alternative: Keep the full pointer-driven effect for every user and device.
decisions.tradeoff: Central control simplifies adaptation; reducing motion amplitude alone does not establish accessibility.
decisions.status: Documented implementation; accessibility boundary is editorial analysis

writingTechniques.technique: Build one visible mechanism at a time.
writingTechniques.evidence: The loader tutorial moves from markup to placement, opacity, and stepped rotation, so each code addition has an observable purpose.

writingTechniques.technique: Include the detour that explains why the simpler solution is better.
writingTechniques.evidence: The easing account preserves the unsuccessful SVG route and credits Archibald's question before showing direct function conversion.

writingTechniques.technique: Make a polished result legible as a series of decisions made by a team.
writingTechniques.evidence: Chrometober names contributors, shows the abandoned concept, and records device-testing and accessibility work rather than presenting the final effect as inevitable.

exercise.task: Create an original five-shape decorative scene with two shared input values and per-shape coefficients. Make normal, reduced, and static variants. Keep adjacent content usable without the decoration. Write a short tutorial that reveals input mapping, one shape, and the full composition in three stages; include one rejected approach.
exercise.deliverable: A small original experiment, a parameter map, screenshots at narrow and wide widths, a motion-preference test record, and a 300-word explanation with credit for borrowed techniques.
evaluation: Can a reader predict what changing one coefficient will do?
Does the static version preserve all information and actions?
Are pointer, non-hover, keyboard, and motion-preference cases considered?
Does the explanation distinguish the author's contribution from libraries, specifications, and collaborators?

limitations: jhey is the public name used here; the articles are bylined Jhey Tompkins.
Chrometober credits Jhey as architectural and creative lead, Tyler Reed for illustration and design, Una Kravets as project lead, and other contributors. It is not a solo project.
Chrometober uses a 2022 experimental API and polyfill. Its syntax and browser-support statements must not be copied as current implementation guidance.

The parallax tutorial's example motion-reduction coefficient is not a universal safe value. Its personal-site original was unavailable through the research tool; the author's DEV syndication was reviewed.
The linear() article credits Jake Archibald's specification and generator work. Jhey's contribution discussed here is the explanation and conversion workflow, not invention of the underlying API.
The compact loader tutorial is not a complete accessible loading-state component. Status semantics, announcements, and motion preferences need separate design.
Demos were read, not executed. Dates for the web.dev articles identify their displayed update dates, not independently verified original publication dates.
people.coverage: Four bylined primary artifacts reviewed, including an author-published syndication, a credited team retrospective, a compact tutorial, and a tool-building account; five decisions and three communication techniques are included.
